For example, 'Ð¯ Ð²Ð¸Ð¶Ñ ÐºÐ½Ð¸Ð³Ñ' (I see the book), 'Ð¯ Ð²Ð¸Ð¶Ñ Ð½ÐµÐ´ÐµÐ»Ñ' (I see the week). For neuter nouns, the accusative is the same as the nominative. For example, 'Ð¯ Ð²Ð¸Ð¶Ñ Ð¾ÐºÐ½Ð¾' (I see the window). For plural nouns, the accusative depends on animacy. Inanimate plurals are the same as nominative. lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Food, Shopping, and Dining Out in Russian

This practical reference supports the RISE AFRICA Skills module Food, Shopping, and Dining Out within the Russian Language course. It is designed for African agribusiness professionals, traders, and entrepreneurs who need to negotiate food purchases, read market prices, order meals, and discuss agricultural products in Russian-speaking environments. The focus is on immediate, business-ready language: quantities, prices, direct objects, and transactional phrases you can use at markets, grocery stores, and restaurants.

Whether you are sourcing wheat from Russia, negotiating sunflower oil contracts, or hosting a business lunch in Moscow, the vocabulary and grammar here will help you move from survival phrases to confident commercial interaction. The module assumes no prior Russian, but it moves quickly toward practical application.

Core Vocabulary and Phrases

Start with high-frequency words that appear in markets, stores, and restaurants. In Russian, nouns have gender, which affects the endings of adjectives and verbs. For business purposes, learn the nominative singular form first, then the accusative form for direct objects.
